Cooling systems. They're responsible for managing the heat generated by electrical components—primarily your CPU and GPU—to prevent thermal damage and keep performance high. Modern systems use either air cooling with heatsinks and fans, or liquid cooling loops. Which one you need depends on your thermal design power, or TDP rating.

Excess heat damages silicon. If components get too hot, the CPU will reduce its clock speed to lower power consumption, a process called thermal throttling. Push it even further and you'll cause permanent failure if the component exceeds 100 to 120 degrees Celsius for sustained periods.

Air cooling uses a heatsink—a metal block usually made of aluminum or copper with fins extending outward to increase surface area. This heatsink mounts directly to the CPU or GPU die. A fan then blows air across those fins to carry heat away from the component.

Between the CPU die and the heatsink sits thermal interface material, or TIM. Usually this is thermal paste or thermal pads. This material fills in the microscopic gaps between the two surfaces to improve contact. If you apply the TIM poorly, cooling efficiency drops dramatically.

Liquid cooling circulates cool fluid through a water block that attaches to the hot component. That fluid then flows through a radiator where a fan cools it back down. Water has much higher heat capacity than air, so liquid cooling is more efficient, especially for high-power CPUs or GPUs.

Thermal Design Power, or TDP, measures in watts the maximum heat a component dissipates at rated conditions. A CPU with a 250-watt TDP requires a heatsink rated for at least that load, with some safety margin built in.

Fan speed is measured in revolutions per minute, or RPM. The volume of air it moves is measured in cubic feet per minute, or CFM. Larger fans can spin slower and still move plenty of air, which keeps them quiet. Smaller fans have to spin faster to move the same amount of air, and they're noisier.

How air circulates through your case matters. Intake fans draw fresh air in. Exhaust fans push hot air out. If you have more exhaust than intake, you create negative pressure, and dust gets sucked in through every crevice. Positive or balanced pressure is ideal.

If you overclock—run your CPU or GPU above stock speeds—you generate significantly more heat. You'll need to increase your cooling capacity proportionally, or the component will thermal throttle and you'll lose the performance gains you wanted in the first place.
